title: Stop Weaponizing Conversational UX
intro: Conversational UX isn't a chatty tone. Moore and Arar's Natural Conversation Framework is about interaction mechanics: turn-taking, context, repair and shared meaning.

learn.title: Four mechanics of a real conversation
learn.text:
**Turn-taking** — respond to what the user just did.
**Context** — fit where they are in the workflow.
**Repair** — help them recover when something breaks.
**Shared meaning** — use the user's words, not the system's internal names.

Framed this way, progressive disclosure is a conversational move: you don't tell a new acquaintance your whole life story.

try.q: Which mechanic does “Something went wrong” fail hardest?
try.explain: It gives the user nothing to recover with.

right.label: Actual conversation
items: Responds to the user's last action

learn.title: The B2B example
learn.text:
A user logs into an analytics tool to export last month's report.

An unrequested tour introduces Workspaces, Automations and Integrations. A modal pushes an upgrade. The export fails with “Something went wrong”. The settings page leads with add-on marketing.

None of it starts from user intent, respects task order, supports repair or builds shared meaning — however friendly the wording is.

try.q: What is wrong with an auto-starting tour, in conversational terms?
options: It ignores what the user came to do
It uses too much text at once
It can't be dismissed on mobile
It repeats information from the signup flow
try.explain: No turn-taking: it starts talking before the user has done anything.

learn.title: The paper test
learn.text:
**1.** Print the words from an onboarding tour, modal, paywall, error or settings page.
**2.** One colleague plays “the system” and may only say what's printed.
**3.** Another plays the user, with a real goal.

If the system can only interrupt, repeat itself, or fail to answer, you have a monologue — and casual wording can disguise interruptions, shaming or upsells.

try.q: In the paper test, what may the person playing the system say?
options: Only the words that are printed
Anything a support agent would say
try.explain: The constraint is the point: it exposes a monologue immediately.

test.q: What is conversational UX actually about?
options: Whether the product has a chatbot
How closely copy matches the brand voice
test.explain: Turn-taking, context, repair and shared meaning.

options: Using the user's words, not system names
Defining key terms in a glossary
Matching the reading level to the audience

test.q: Why is progressive disclosure a conversational move?
options: You don't tell a new acquaintance everything at once
It reduces the number of words on screen
It lets users set their own pace
It mirrors how chatbots stream responses
test.explain: Information arrives when it is relevant to the exchange.
Which is why the test is whether the language helps the task.
